draft.title: Global influences on policy
card: Australia is a small open economy. It trades a lot with the world and borrows from overseas, but it is a small part of the world economy.
Because of this, Australia is a price taker. It cannot set world prices for goods such as iron ore, or world interest rates. Events overseas can change Australian incomes and jobs.
A global event, such as a recession in a major trading partner, can cut demand for Australian exports. It may do more to slow growth than a domestic policy does to lift it.
Other countries' policies also matter. If major economies raise interest rates, funds may move overseas and the Australian dollar may fall. This can limit what Australian policy achieves.
draft.remember: Australia is small and open, so world events can outweigh its own policy.

a.q: Why can world events outweigh domestic policy in Australia?
opts: Australia is a small open economy and a price taker
Australia has no control over its own interest rates
Australian policy never affects output or employment
Australia trades with only a few countries overseas
a.why: Australia is a small part of a large world economy, so it cannot set world prices or demand. Policy still has effects at home. The claim that it has no control or never works goes too far, because global events only can outweigh it.
a.clue: Think about Australia's size compared with the world economy.

b.q: The Reserve Bank lowers the cash rate to lift growth in Australia. At the same time, a recession in major trading partners cuts demand for Australian exports. What is the most likely result?
opts: Growth is lifted by less than the policy alone would suggest
Growth rises by more because exports are cheaper to buy
Growth is unchanged because monetary policy has no effect
Growth falls to zero because policy always fails
b.why: The lower cash rate pushes growth up, but weaker export demand from overseas pulls it down. The overseas shock offsets part of the policy, so growth rises by less than expected. It does not cancel the policy completely, and policy does not always fail.
b.clue: Two forces act on growth: one at home and one from overseas.

a.best: Australia is a small open economy and a price taker

b.best: Growth is lifted by less than the policy alone would suggest

problems.detail: The card says a global recession 'may do more to slow growth than a domestic policy does to lift it', so overall growth could fall. The intended answer says growth is still 'lifted', and the why says the shock 'does not cancel the policy completely'. Both contradict the card's main idea that world events can outweigh domestic policy.

The question gives no sizes for the two effects, so 'most likely result' cannot be settled. 'Lifted by less' is only safe if read as 'growth is lower than with the policy alone'. Reword it, for example: 'growth is weaker than the rate cut alone would give'.
The wrong option 'Australian policy never affects output or employment' uses an absolute word. Students can rule it out without knowing the idea.
Two wrong options rest on absolutes ('policy always fails', 'has no effect'). Students can rule them out without knowing the idea, which leaves the right answer too easy to spot.
The why (a) phrase 'global events only can outweigh it' is ungrammatical and confusing. It should read 'global events can only sometimes outweigh it' or 'global events can outweigh it'.
